s: A tasting-menu counter and dining room built around a single evolving Korean course sequence, numbered rather than named.
w: Junghyun and Ellia Park's Michelin two-star dining room serves a numbered, ever-changing tasting menu inspired by hansik. The room is split between an upstairs dining room and a downstairs counter facing the kitchen; it has held two Michelin stars since 2021 and was ranked among the World's 50 Best Restaurants.
_facts: Chefs Junghyun 'JP' Park and Ellia Park
Two Michelin stars
World's 50 Best Restaurants list

s: A narrow counter-and-booth diner under the Manhattan Bridge overpass, reworking classic plate-lunch fare through an Asian-American lens.
w: Chef Sam Yoo took over a decades-old Two Bridges diner shell and kept the linoleum-and-counter-stool bones while rebuilding the menu around dishes like a kimchi-studded smash burger and scallion pancake breakfast sandwiches, tucked under the Manhattan Bridge approach.
_facts: Chef-owner Sam Yoo
Occupies a former classic NYC diner space under the Manhattan Bridge

a: E Houston St, Lower East Side
s: A cafeteria-style deli on the corner of Houston and Ludlow, ticket-in-hand ordering and hand-carved pastrami on rye since 1888.
w: Founded in 1888 and run by the Dell'Aquila-Kaufman family since 1988, Katz's still works the way it always has: take a ticket at the door, queue at the counter, tip the carver. The pastrami is hand-cut, cured and smoked in-house. It's the deli behind the 'I'll have what she's having' scene in When Harry Met Sally.
_facts: Founded 1888, oldest continuously operating deli in NYC
Setting of the famous scene from When Harry Met Sally

s: A Nolita corner diner from the Uncle Boons team, running Thai-American mash-ups like massaman disco fries under a classic checkerboard floor.
w: Opened in 2020 by chefs behind the shuttered Uncle Boons, Thai Diner reworks the American diner playbook -- meatloaf, French toast, disco fries -- through Thai technique. The Thai tea babka French toast and massaman-curry disco fries are the two dishes it's known for citywide. Holds a Michelin Bib Gourmand.
_facts: Opened 2020 by the team behind the now-closed Uncle Boons
Michelin Bib Gourmand

s: The first permanent outpost outside Italy of Rome's century-old Roscioli deli-restaurant, built around a salumi-and-cheese counter in the South Village.
w: Roscioli began as a Rome bakery-turned-deli on Via dei Giubbonari; the New York room, opened in 2023 on MacDougal Street, is the family's first location anywhere outside Italy. The menu keeps the Roman deli's spine -- cacio e pepe, carbonara, a case of imported salumi and cheese.
_facts: First permanent Roscioli location outside Italy, opened 2023
Sister operation to the original Roscioli in Rome

s: A century-old Village tavern, its caricature-lined walls intact, rebuilt by Keith McNally around a famously rich Black Label burger.
w: Minetta Tavern has occupied this MacDougal Street corner since 1937, its walls hung with decades of Village caricatures. Keith McNally reopened it in 2009 as a Parisian-tinged steakhouse, adding a dry-aged program built around the Black Label burger, a blend of short rib, brisket and skirt steak. Holds a Michelin star.
_facts: Original tavern dates to 1937; reopened by Keith McNally in 2009
Michelin-starred
Known for the Black Label burger

s: A stand-up slice shop on Carmine Street, folding thin, foldable New York slices since 1975.
w: Joe Pozzuoli opened this Carmine Street storefront in 1975 and it has run more or less the same way ever since: a short counter, slices sold plain or fresh mozzarella, eaten standing or walking. It's the location used as the Peter Parker's workplace stand-in in the Spider-Man films.
_facts: Opened 1975 by Joe Pozzuoli
Used as a filming location for Spider-Man

s: A takeout-window pizzeria on Prince Street, known for a thick square Sicilian slice with a pepperoni cup crisped at the edges.
w: Prince Street Pizza's signature is the Spicy Spring, a square Sicilian-style slice topped with cupped pepperoni that curls and crisps under the broiler. The Nolita storefront, run by the DeMarco family, has been slinging slices from a narrow takeout counter for decades. No seating inside.
_facts: Signature item: the 'Spicy Spring' square pepperoni slice
Family-run by the DeMarco family

s: A glass-fronted West Village Italian on a quiet residential block, built around house-made pasta and an open kitchen counter.
w: L'Artusi opened in 2008 on a tree-lined stretch of West 10th Street, its floor-to-ceiling windows and marble counter seating facing straight into the pasta station. The kitchen turns out modern Italian plates alongside a rotating pasta list and wood-grilled branzino.
_facts: Opened 2008
Sibling restaurant to Dell'Anima and Anfora

s: A no-reservations West Village trattoria near Sheridan Square, its market-driven Italian plates and short bar built around communal patience.
w: Chefs Jody Williams and Rita Sodi opened Via Carota in 2014 on a Grove Street corner near Sheridan Square, running it as a no-reservations trattoria where a wait at the small bar is part of the ritual. The insalata verde and cacio e pepe are the most-ordered dishes, cooked from a kitchen with no walk-in freezer.
_facts: Opened 2014 by chefs Jody Williams and Rita Sodi
No-reservations policy

s: A Roman and Williams-designed SoHo dining room where chef Daniel Rose plates old-guard French dishes with unusual precision.
w: Daniel Rose, a Chicago-born chef who built his reputation running Spring in Paris, opened Le Coucou in 2016 with restaurateur Stephen Starr, inside a Roman and Williams room of vaulted ceilings and toile wallpaper. The menu revives dishes largely absent from New York's French restaurant scene -- quenelles, sweetbreads, a whole roasted chicken for two.
_facts: Opened 2016, chef Daniel Rose with Stephen Starr
Interior designed by Roman and Williams
Michelin-starred

s: Rich Torrisi's Nolita dining room, a tasting-menu reworking of Italian-American classics from a Major Food Group founder.
w: Torrisi reopened under chef Rich Torrisi's sole direction in December 2022 on Mulberry Street. The tasting menu moves through Italian-American staples -- chicken parm, veal, a martini course -- reworked with tasting-menu precision. Earned a Michelin star in 2023.
_facts: Reopened under chef Rich Torrisi, December 2022
Co-founder of Major Food Group
Michelin star since 2023

s: A red-sauce Italian-American theatre on Thompson Street, tuxedoed captains working tableside carts of veal parm and Caesar salad.
w: Mario Carbone, Rich Torrisi and Jeff Zalaznick opened Carbone in 2013 in a former red-sauce joint's shell, keeping the checkerboard floor while staffing the room with captains in white dinner jackets. The spicy rigatoni vodka and veal parmesan are the dishes it's known for, alongside a reservation waitlist that's a running citywide joke.
_facts: Opened 2013, Major Food Group
Michelin-starred since 2018
Famous for reservation scarcity

s: A single-room, BYOB pizzeria on a residential Carroll Gardens corner, thin pies hand-stretched in view of the whole dining room.
w: Mark Iacono converted a former candy store on Henry Street into Lucali in 2006, keeping the room down to a single pizza oven and a scattering of tables, with a no-reservations, cash-and-BYOB policy that hasn't changed since. Pies are stretched and topped in full view at the front counter, thin-crusted and lightly charred.
_facts: Opened 2006 by Mark Iacono
BYOB, cash-friendly, no reservations
Closed Tuesdays

s: A Midwood corner pizzeria running since 1965, its pies still finished with hand-snipped basil and a swirl of olive oil.
w: Domenico DeMarco opened Di Fara on Avenue J in 1965 and worked the oven himself for nearly five decades, building a reputation on slow-made pies finished tableside with scissor-cut basil, grated Parmesan and a final swirl of oil. He died in 2019; the DeMarco family now runs the kitchen following his methods.
_facts: Opened 1965 by Domenico DeMarco
DeMarco died 2019; family continues to run it

s: The 2003 South Lamar bungalow where Tyson Cole rewired Austin's idea of sushi, before the name spread to a dozen other cities.
w: Uchi opened in 2003 inside a converted house on South Lamar; the name is simply Japanese for 'home.' Tyson Cole's cooking, hot and cold small plates built around daily fish deliveries, won him the James Beard Award for Best Chef Southwest in 2011 and eventually spawned outposts across the country. This is still the original room where the format began.
_facts: Founded 2003 by chef Tyson Cole
Cole won James Beard Best Chef Southwest, 2011
Original/flagship location

s: A Lower Greenville beer garden built around a lit-up treehouse bar, with food trucks rotating in under the oaks.
w: Jason Boso opened Truck Yard on Sears Street in 2013, filling roughly 15,000 square feet of yard with picnic tables, an Airstream bar, string lights and a treehouse that's become the photo people come for. Food trucks rotate through rather than a fixed kitchen.
_facts: Opened 2013 by Jason Boso
~15,000 sq ft outdoor beer garden with rotating food trucks and a treehouse bar

s: Kevin Kelley bought the historic Hart Building outright on Elm Street when no downtown landlord would lease him space for Southern comfort food.
w: A former litigation attorney, Kevin Kelley conceived Kitchen + Kocktails while living in Paris and missing the soul food of home. Unable to secure a downtown Dallas lease, he bought the century-old Hart Building on Elm Street and opened there in 2020. The menu runs chicken and waffles, Caribbean jerk lamb chops, oxtails and candied yams.
_facts: Founder/chef Kevin Kelley, a former litigation attorney
Opened 2020 in the historic Hart Building

s: Aaron Franklin's East 11th Street smokehouse, where the brisket line has been forming since 2009.
w: Franklin opened his trailer-turned-restaurant on East 11th Street in 2009 and became, in 2015, the first pitmaster to win the James Beard Award for Best Chef Southwest. The brisket -- post-oak smoked, salted and peppered and nothing else -- still sells out most days before the line finishes moving.
_facts: Opened 2009 by Aaron and Stacy Franklin
First pitmaster to win a James Beard 'Best Chef' award, 2015
Obama bought the whole line lunch, July 2014

a: E Cesar Chavez St, East Austin
s: Ali Clem's brisket, cooked eight hours over post oak, at the East Cesar Chavez lot she built with LeAnn Mueller.
w: Clem was hired by pitmaster John Mueller to run a trailer on South First before she and LeAnn Mueller -- daughter of Bobby Mueller, a James Beard-winning barbecue pioneer -- built La Barbecue into its current form. The brisket runs low and slow for roughly eight hours over Texas post oak.
_facts: Pitmaster/owner Ali Clem, co-built with LeAnn Mueller
Michelin Guide-recommended

s: Brandon Hurtado's Central Texas brisket, smoked out of a 120-year-old former railroad depot in downtown Arlington.
w: Brandon and Hannah Hurtado opened Hurtado Barbecue in 2020 inside a former Front Street railroad depot, more than a century old. The kitchen runs Central Texas brisket alongside Tex-Mex fusion plates, and holds the concession contract as the official barbecue of the Texas Rangers at Globe Life Field.
_facts: Founded 2020 by Brandon and Hannah Hurtado
Official BBQ of the Texas Rangers
In a 120-year-old former railroad depot

s: The original Truluck's, on Westheimer since 1992, still running trap-to-table stone crab under twenty-four hours old.
w: Truluck's opened its first location on Westheimer Road in 1992, built around Florida stone crab caught and served within a day, and USDA Prime steaks. It remains privately held by its two founders, with the chain since spreading across Texas -- but Westheimer is where it started.
_facts: Founded 1992, privately held
Signature: Florida stone crab, trap-to-table under 24 hours

s: A family scratch kitchen on Elm Street downtown, named for the owner's daughter, working oxtails and a salmon-and-shrimp pasta locals rate among the city's best.
w: Kendall's Soul Food runs a small storefront on Elm Street in downtown Dallas, near JFK Memorial Plaza, cooking from scratch under a name taken from the owner's daughter. The kitchen leans into oxtails, ribs, cornbread and a salmon-and-shrimp pasta over garlic penne.
_facts: Family-owned scratch kitchen, named after the owner's daughter
Known for oxtails and salmon-and-shrimp garlic-penne pasta

s: The Hutchins family's flagship smokehouse on North Tennessee Street, running since they moved the operation off the family homeplace in 1991.
w: Roy and Delores Hutchins started smoking barbecue attached to their home in Princeton in 1978, then moved the operation to its current North Tennessee Street site in McKinney in 1991. Now run by their children, the kitchen has cooked at the James Beard House twice and put up a Texas Twinkie -- a bacon-wrapped jalapeño stuffed with brisket and cream cheese.
_facts: Founded 1978 in Princeton, TX; moved to McKinney 1991
Cooked twice at the James Beard House
